cur:manuscripts-khludov-transfiguration.summary: At the top of a steep red mountain, Christ stands in a blue mandorla between Moses and Elijah, while on the slopes below the three apostles fall to the ground, dazzled by the light. The tall, narrow composition fits the margin of the page beside the psalm text it illuminates.
facts: Byzantine marginal psalters commonly attached the Transfiguration to the verse 'Tabor and Hermon shall rejoice in thy name' (Psalm 88:13 in the Septuagint).
The Khludov Psalter contains 169 folios and measures about 195 by 150 mm.
cur:manuscripts-khludov-transfiguration.notes: The specific psalm verse beside this miniature is not legible in the low-resolution image; the Tabor association is the usual one in this tradition.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-67-christ.summary: At the top of a crowded page the beardless Christ-Logos rides out of the clouds in a four-horse chariot among angels, brandishing a spear, from the verse about 'the chariots of God'; the psalm's 'thou hast ascended on high' was applied to the Ascension. The bearded psalmist stands in the middle pointing to the many episodes around him, from a procession of musicians to animals and kings. The instruments drawn here are often cited by music historians.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
Its text is written in rustic capitals, an archaic script that once led scholars to date the manuscript to the 6th century; the drawings are now recognised as Carolingian.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-67-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-127-chris.summary: On a hill within the enclosure the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos with three angels raises his hand in blessing toward a king and queen eating 'the labour of thine hands' at a table, beneath a vine on a trellis, with children beside olive trees — 'thy children like olive plants round about thy table'. Outside the wall the labours that produced their food are shown. The lower drawing of folio 73v gives a gentle picture of the blessed household.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
The psalter was made in or near Reims, probably under Archbishop Ebbo (816–835); some scholars argue for a date around 850 under his successor Hincmar.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-127-chris.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server. This folio carries two drawings; the crop shows the one for this text.

cur:objects-berlin-crucifixion-with-sold.summary: Christ is crucified high in the upper part of the panel, with mourning angels above the cross. Below, the Virgin and the holy women stand at the left, while at the right a group of helmeted soldiers gathers. The fuller, more narrative version of Calvary contrasts the sorrow of the faithful with the indifference of the executioners.
facts: Byzantine ivory carvers produced both the simple three-figure Crucifixion and fuller narrative versions with soldiers and mourners, sometimes in the same workshop (type).

Q546297.summary: The body of Christ lies on a marble slab, seen from his pierced feet with dramatic foreshortening, while the Virgin, Saint John and Mary Magdalene weep at the edge of the picture. The muted palette and unflinching closeness give the scene the quality of a vigil beside the body. It is one of the most daring and moving images of the Renaissance.
facts: Mantegna deliberately reduced the size of Christ's feet; true perspective would have made them large enough to hide much of the body.
A 'foreshortened Christ' is recorded among the works left in Mantegna's studio at his death in 1506, possibly kept for his own devotion; it was soon acquired by Cardinal Sigismondo Gonzaga.
The slab is thought to represent the Stone of Unction on which Christ's body was anointed for burial.
